claim: Confidence is built from cues (fluency, ease, amount of partial information, self-consistency), not read from memory. Cues that are valid in the usual case mislead when ease and accuracy come apart.
agent_test: Plant misleading cues (long fluent wrong rationale vs short correct one) and check whether the agent's confidence follows fluency; compare to a confidence taken from sample agreement at equal tokens.

claim: Delaying the judgment (or making it from a fresh retrieval attempt) sharply improves resolution of learning judgments (g=0.93 on gamma, 4,554 people) with almost no memory effect (g=0.08). Gap search re-read the meta-analysis abstract record: 4,554 people / 112 effect sizes g=0.93 on relative accuracy; 3,807 people / 98 effect sizes g=0.08 on memory. The effect depends on the cue: strong when the cue is the stimulus alone, near zero when the cue is stimulus plus answer (d17). Full text and moderator tables not read.
agent_test: Ask for confidence right after answering vs after a separate fresh re-solve; compare AUROC at equal total tokens.

claim: Overconfidence on hard sets and the hard-easy effect are partly a sampling artefact: on representative item sets overconfidence mostly vanishes; the pattern is also predicted by regression to the mean and noise. Gap search: a preregistered 11-model study finds the hard-easy pattern in LLMs (reasoning-model slope 0.168 vs chat 0.732) but attributes it to regression to the mean without testing it, on non-representative sets (d04). So the pattern exists; its cause is still open.
schema_part: G (do not assume bias; measure on own distribution)
agent_test: Measure agent calibration on a representative mix vs a hand-picked hard set; check whether bias flips sign with difficulty.

claim: The Dunning-Kruger quartile pattern is largely a statistical artefact; in large samples the relation between self-estimate and skill is close to linear and extra low-skill miscalibration is small (quadratic dR2 .011 at N=13,977).
agent_test: Not worth a test. Do not build a 'weaker model is more overconfident' rule on this literature; test directly on LLMs (see K12).

claim: Confidence and accuracy can reverse: for consistently wrong items, higher confidence goes with lower accuracy. Reliability (consistency) differs from validity (correctness). Only one lab reports this, and one statistic in it was not reconciled. The wider consistent-and-wrong failure (not the sign reversal) is now backed by two more independent sources, see K20.
schema_part: G (confidence must not be the sole stop signal)
agent_test: On items where samples agree on a wrong answer, check whether confidence ranks them above correct but variable items.

claim: Feeling of rightness and feeling of error are cheap, fast signals that predict whether a second look happens and whether an intuitive answer is changed; they are driven by answer fluency and conflict.
agent_test: Trigger a verification pass only when a cheap first-pass signal (token entropy, disagreement of 2 cheap samples) is low; compare to always verifying at equal tokens.

claim: Verbalised LLM confidence is poorly separated: it clusters at 80-100%, and GPT-4 average AUROC across 8 datasets is only 62.7% (chance 50%). A low ECE can come from giving 100% to everything when accuracy is high (GSM8K, GPT-4 CoT, 93.6% acc, ECE 0.064, no discrimination). Re-checked in the paper text.
schema_part: G (never use raw verbal confidence alone); O (verify)
agent_test: Report AUROC next to ECE for every confidence signal the agent uses; reject signals with AUROC under 0.65.

claim: Agreement across several samples predicts correctness much better than one verbalised number. GSM8K AUROC for GPT-3.5 went from 54.8% (one verbalised answer) to 92.7% (5 samples with consistency); 5-dataset average 56.4% to 73.0%. Semantic entropy beats a plain count of distinct answers (AUROC .77 vs .66 CoQA; .83 vs .79 TriviaQA). All re-checked in the source tables. Limits from the gap search: in agent tasks agreement AUROC is 0.62 to 0.78 (d09), and in a GPQA audit the link between consistency and correctness is weak (Spearman 0.20 to 0.59, d10).
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare 1 long reasoning + verbal confidence vs 4 shorter samples with agreement as confidence: AUROC and selective accuracy.

claim: On RLHF chat models, asking for verbalised confidence (a number, with top-k guesses) beats the token probability for calibration. gpt-3.5 TriviaQA ECE 0.140 (label prob) vs 0.050 (verbalised top-2); SciQ 0.256 vs 0.065 (top-4); TruthfulQA 0.451 vs 0.203. Discrimination stays weak (TruthfulQA AUC about 0.45-0.55). Re-checked against the paper table.
agent_test: Compare confidence prompts (single number, top-2 with probabilities, binary) on the agent's own tasks at equal tokens.

claim: Sampling/token methods give good ECE but weak AUROC; verbal elicitation gives decent AUROC but poor ECE. Finetuning on about 1,000 to 5,000 graded examples beats prompting. That needs training, which is outside our no-training constraint; a post-hoc recalibration map is allowed.
schema_part: none for training; G for recalibration map
agent_test: Fit a cheap post-hoc mapping (isotonic) from raw signal to correctness on 200 held-out items; check the drop in ECE on a different 200.

claim: Reasoning models (thinking mode) state better-calibrated confidence than non-thinking versions in the same family. Table 1 of Yoon et al. now read row by row: TriviaQA ECE Qwen3-32B 0.207 (non-thinking) to 0.063 (thinking); Qwen2.5-32B-Inst 0.129 to R1-Distill-Qwen 0.042; GLM-4 0.084 to GLM-Z1 0.029. The Qwen3 Thinking row is identical to the QwQ row in every cell (possible copy error). Ablation (no CoT 0.150, non-linear reasoning removed 0.161, original 0.042) points to slow exploratory reasoning as the cause. The effect is task dependent: Zeng et al. find reasoning fine-tuning worsens calibration on factual QA for small open models while improving it on AIME (ECE 0.752 to 0.240); a small-model study shows accuracy and ECE can move in opposite directions. No closed frontier model checked.
schema_part: S (give confidence after reasoning, not before)
agent_test: Elicit confidence before vs after the reasoning phase at equal tokens.

claim: Models show high confidence regardless of evidence or difficulty. In debates both sides report about 73% initial confidence (rational 50%); on a hard task confidence was 34% vs accuracy 10%; one model had accuracy 23.3% with confidence 95.7%. Reasoning models track actual probability better (r=.94 vs .48 for chat models).
schema_part: G (distrust self-assessed confidence on hard, novel items)
agent_test: Run the agent on both sides of an adversarial 2-sided task and see if its confidences sum above 100%.

claim: Confidence wording changes how readers act and is itself unreliable. Strengtheners accompanied 53% correct answers and weakeners 32%, yet 17% of wrong answers carried strengtheners (9 models, 125,244 queries; re-checked). Readers of default explanations discriminate at AUC about .59 while model confidence has AUC about .75 (re-checked); longer explanations widen the gap.
schema_part: G (output style: do not let explanation length stand in for confidence)
agent_test: Compare the agent's answers with short vs long justifications and test whether a downstream judge's accuracy changes.

claim: Self-correction without external feedback does not reliably help reasoning and may hurt (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1), because the model has no signal for which answers are wrong. Confidence-gated revision (revise only when confidence is low) is the proposed fix and shows gains in cascades.
schema_part: O (revise only on a trigger) / G
agent_test: Compare always-revise vs revise-when-signal-low at equal tokens.

claim: Confidence-guided test-time scaling saves samples: at budget 5/10, P(True) cut cost 41%/46% vs plain self-consistency; a search-agent study reached higher accuracy with fewer attempts (BrowseComp 54.5 with 3.87 attempts vs 47.5 for 10-sample self-consistency).
schema_part: O (stopping rule) / links to adaptive stopping
agent_test: Implement confidence-weighted vote with early stop and compare to fixed N at equal mean tokens.

claim: Reported LLM calibration numbers are unstable across protocol details: the token-score context flips the best method in 4 of 12 settings (ECE) and 9 of 12 (AUROC); accepting an alias instead of the canonical answer shifts verbal confidence by 0.072; metacognitive efficiency correlates with accuracy -0.80 on one dataset and 0.00 on another.
agent_test: Re-run the calibration measurement with three prompt formats and see if the rank of methods changes.

claim: Models predict their own correctness only slightly better than a different model of similar skill predicts it, and a trained confidence head transfers only partly to new domains (out-of-domain TruthfulQA ECE worsened .10 to .18). Gap search: transfer of an agent calibrator to a new domain is partial (MMLU-Pro to HLE ECE 0.504; pooled calibrator tested on GAIA gets better ECE but worse AUROC, d05); per-slice recalibration beats one global map, ECE 0.063 / 0.063 / 0.053 for base / global / per-slice on MMLU (d11).
agent_test: Check whether a calibration map fitted on one task family holds on another.

claim: LLMs do not show human-like cue sensitivity of judgments of learning in one garden-path task: slope of JOL on recognition near 0 for GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o (B .013 to .045, CI includes 0) vs humans B=.167. One preprint.
agent_test: None needed; do not import human metamemory results to LLMs without a check.

claim: Faithfulness of verbal hedges is low: vanilla conditional faithful generation is about 0.5, the value of ignoring confidence. Decisions made from verbal confidence yield utility gains on hard benchmarks (HLE) but none on easy ones (GSM8K).
agent_test: Check whether the agent's action (abstain, verify, answer) actually changes with its stated confidence.

claim: A stable share of tasks are answered wrongly and consistently. In tool-using agents 5.5% to 10% of tasks are consistent-wrong, which caps what agreement-based filtering can gain (d09). On GPQA a strong GPT-4.1 tier is wrong on 48% of cases where consistency is at least 0.8, and 28% of items are confidently wrong for every runner (8% to 15% for smaller tiers). Models from different families give the same wrong answer more often than chance (Haiku 10 of 15, p=.003). More samples or a second model do not remove it.
schema_part: G (no verdict from agreement alone) / O verify
agent_test: Seed items where the model is known to be confidently wrong; measure how many pass an agreement gate; then check whether an outside test, tool, or a different-method re-solve catches them.

claim: Confidence stated after reasoning discriminates only when real reasoning came first. R1-32B verbal AUROC is 0.56 with no reasoning, 0.80 after 100 to 500 tokens, up to 0.88 with long forced reasoning, matching semantic entropy from 10 samples (270 items). Qwen3 thinking vs non-thinking AUROC 0.650 to 0.807. A reader model that sees only the trace recovers the same score, so the stated number mostly summarises the trace.
agent_test: Elicit confidence (a) right after a no-reasoning answer, (b) after the full trace, (c) after a blind re-solve; compare AUROC on our graded tasks at equal tokens.

claim: In multi-step coding agents stated success probability is far above real success and discriminates weakly: AUROC 0.51 to 0.64 (Pre/post-run, SWE-bench Pro, N=100); asking before the work is as good as asking after; overconfidence of several models grows as the task proceeds; whole-run verbalised AUROC is 0.59 to 0.66 on GPQA/HLE/SimpleQA agent runs. Decisions follow the stated probability closely, so wrong confidence turns directly into wrong action.
schema_part: G (confidence is not a verdict) / S checkpoint
agent_test: Log stated confidence at each checkpoint of a multi-step run and the final outcome; compute AUROC per step and the act/abstain/verify decision rate by confidence bin.

claim: Cheap triggers exist that need no extra full samples: local token-confidence dips (lowest group or tail of a trace) with a 16-trace warm-up (up to 84.7% fewer tokens, accuracy kept or raised), and stopping when a small window of early samples agrees (67% to 84% fewer samples on easy sets, 34% on MATH). Both are fluency or agreement cues and fail on confident-wrong traces (top-10% filtering lowers accuracy in 8 of 20 settings). No study tests them as a gate for re-examination in a multi-step agent, and none compares at equal tokens against one long trace.
agent_test: Compare three triggers for a verify step at equal tokens: token-confidence dip, disagreement of two early samples, and stated confidence after reasoning.

claim: The delayed-JOL analogue for an LLM is a blind re-solve from the question alone, not a re-read of question plus its own answer. Human delayed JOL helps strongly with a stimulus-only cue (all 45 subjects) and hardly with a stimulus-plus-answer cue. Nobody has tested the LLM version with current reasoning models; the nearest result (adversarial post-run review) shifts calibration but costs about twice as much and gives non-significant AUROC changes.
agent_test: Judge correctness (a) with the answer visible and (b) after a fresh re-solve that never sees the first answer; compare AUROC and token cost.

claim: Calibration maps should be per task type, not global, and need labelled runs from the target slice. Per-slice recalibration beat global temperature scaling in every setting tested (MMLU ECE 0.063 to 0.053 at PaLM2-L; 0.109 to 0.074 at LLaMA-65B) and still gave useful gains from 5 to 20 items per slice; an agent calibrator learned on one domain transferred only partly (several hundred labelled runs per domain were used). How many held-out items a counting-table map needs without training is not measured.
agent_test: Build a bin-count lookup from n = 25, 50, 100, 200 graded runs per task type; report ECE on held-out runs and under task-type shift.

claim: Reasoning models show a much smaller hard-easy slope than chat models (0.168 vs 0.732 aggregate; reasoning ECE 0.037 vs 0.150 over 11 models). A difficulty-dependent confidence correction is therefore low priority for a reasoning-model agent. Single preprint, no uncertainty on the coefficients.
schema_part: G (do not assume bias; measure on own distribution)
agent_test: Bin our graded tasks by difficulty proxy and check whether the calibration gap depends on bin before adding any correction.

claim: Having the agent score its own work is biased toward itself: GPT scored its own patches 23 points higher than others' (N=25, p=0.001). An adversarial review frame cut overconfident failures from 72% to 45% but cost 12.7 to 23.4 steps per task. Platt scaling alone brought one model's ECE to 0.01 without improving AUROC.
agent_test: Check whether verification by a fresh instance with an adversarial frame beats same-context self-review at equal cost.
